facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Jo March was the most unusual of the four sisters in almost every way that mattered most to her. She hated sewing and dancing and all the things that young ladies in her time were supposed to love. She loved running and writing and having adventures and arguing about interesting ideas with people. When Laurie asked her to marry him she said no even though everyone around her expected her to say yes. When a publisher rejected her stories she rewrote them and sent them out again without self-pity. Jo refused to become the person that society said a young woman should be at that time. Jo refused society's expectations.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Jo March knew from a very young age that she was not going to fit into the life that her era had planned for women. She was too loud, too ambitious, too comfortable with conflict, and too interested in the world outside her home. She burned with the desire to write stories that mattered — not domestic sketches but real stories with real ideas in them. When she sent her first real story to a publisher and it was rejected she felt the disappointment like a physical blow. But she sat back down at her desk and rewrote it because the alternative — giving up and becoming conventional — was unthinkable. Jo's relationship with her own ambition was one of the most honest portraits of female intellectual life in nineteenth-century fiction. She wanted something that her world told her she could not have and she pursued it with complete and unapologetic dedication. Jo refused society's expectations.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Jo March is one of the most enduring characters in American literature precisely because of the specific quality of her refusal. She does not refuse society's expectations out of abstract principle or theoretical feminism — she refuses them because they fit her badly. Her ambition is not a political position; it is a personal necessity as real and as urgent as hunger or thirst. Alcott understood something important about the nature of authentic rebellion: it is not chosen but discovered through self-knowledge. Jo does not become a writer to make a point — she becomes a writer because the alternative is a slow suffocation of everything she is. Her refusal of Laurie is the most dramatic expression of this self-knowledge — she will not trade her truest self for comfort and connection. She will find her own way or she will not find it at all, and she accepts this condition with her eyes fully and clearly open. That willingness to pay the real cost of refusing is what separates genuine self-determination from mere stubbornness or eccentricity. Jo refused society's expectations.
